Pregnancy

Twin birthweight: what the numbers mean

Updated: October 7, 2026

Written and edited by BeMama Authors team: checked against published guidance from recognized health organizations.

Twins are often born earlier and smaller than single babies, but there is no fixed weight that every twin must reach. The important questions are how each baby is growing, how their placenta and sac arrangement affects care, and when birth is safest for this pregnancy.

There is no single correct birthweight for twins

Parents expecting twins often hear a number described as the weight their babies should reach. In reality, birthweight varies with gestational age, each baby’s growth and the pregnancy circumstances. Twins can weigh more than 2.4 kg at birth; that figure is not an upper limit. A smaller weight is also not, by itself, a complete prediction of how a baby will do.

Low birthweight means a weight below 2,500 g, regardless of the week of birth. Prematurity means birth before 37 completed weeks. They describe different things: a baby may be small because they were born early, because growth was restricted, or both. A baby born at term can also have a low birthweight.

Ask about each baby separately. A combined weight for the pair, or a comparison with a friend’s singleton baby, does not show whether either twin has followed an appropriate growth pattern. Ultrasound weights before birth are estimates, not measurements from a scale.

Why the placenta and amniotic sacs matter

An early ultrasound aims to establish how many placentas and amniotic sacs there are. This information helps determine the monitoring plan. Whether twins are identical is interesting for families, but the placenta and sac arrangement is especially important for medical care.

Dichorionic diamniotic twins, often shortened to DCDA, each have a placenta and a separate sac. They avoid the specific blood-sharing problem of a shared placenta, but still need twin-pregnancy care. DCDA twins may be non-identical or identical; two placentas do not automatically answer that question.

Monochorionic diamniotic twins, or MCDA, share a placenta but have separate sacs. They are usually described as identical twins. Shared placental circulation brings extra risks, including twin–twin transfusion syndrome, and closer ultrasound surveillance is needed. Being identical does not mean that growth or health will be identical.

Monochorionic monoamniotic twins, or MCMA, share both the placenta and a sac. This is uncommon and requires specialist care, including attention to the umbilical cords, which can become entangled. It is more helpful to understand the extra monitoring and birth plan than to describe this pregnancy simply as the “worst” type.

Earlier birth is one reason twins are often smaller

Twins have a greater chance of arriving before 37 weeks. Earlier birth leaves less time for weight gain in the uterus, even when growth until that point has been appropriate. Some births follow spontaneous labour; others are planned because the balance of risk favours delivery.

The aim is not always to continue to a singleton due date. As an example, NICE recommends planned birth for uncomplicated DCDA twins at 37 weeks, MCDA twins at 36 weeks, and MCMA twins between 32 weeks and 33 weeks plus 6 days. These are UK guideline examples, not instructions to schedule your own birth; local recommendations and complications can change the plan.

A care team considers growth, fluid, placental function, the pregnant person’s health and neonatal support. Waiting only to reach a target weight can be unsafe if there are other concerns. Ask why the proposed timing is appropriate for your particular type of twin pregnancy.

Growth restriction and unequal growth

Fetal growth restriction means a baby is not reaching their expected growth potential. It is different from simply having a smaller estimated weight than their co-twin. Placental function, how a shared placenta is divided, and cord-related factors can affect the supply of oxygen and nutrients to each baby.

One twin may therefore grow more slowly than the other, although a difference between them does not automatically prove a dangerous problem. Clinicians consider the size of the difference, each baby’s growth over time and the rest of the scan findings. A single estimated weight cannot answer all of those questions.

Monitoring may include measurements of both babies, amniotic fluid around each one and Doppler assessment of blood flow. Concern about growth can mean more frequent checks or referral to fetal medicine. The team should explain what has changed, what it might mean and what would lead to a different delivery plan.

Maternal health and other pregnancy complications

Twin pregnancy also calls for attention to the pregnant person’s blood pressure, blood count and other routine assessments. Conditions such as hypertension or pre-eclampsia may affect placental function and the timing of birth. Gestational diabetes is another concern in multiple pregnancy, but it does not have a single predictable effect of making babies smaller.

Problems involving fluid, cords or a baby’s development may also affect care. The purpose of scans and appointments is to look for these issues and respond, not to suggest that every twin pregnancy will have them. Many families have healthy outcomes with the appropriate monitoring.

Twins do not automatically require a caesarean birth. The type of pregnancy, position of the babies, gestation, complications and your preferences all inform that discussion. A recommendation for an operation should be explained in relation to those findings rather than treated as a consequence of being pregnant with twins alone.

Twin–twin transfusion syndrome is more than a weight difference

Twin–twin transfusion syndrome, or TTTS, can occur when twins share a placenta with connecting blood vessels. An imbalance in blood flow can leave the donor twin with too little circulating blood and place strain on the recipient twin. The donor may make less urine and have less fluid around them, while the recipient can have excess fluid and cardiovascular strain.

This is not diagnosed simply because one twin is heavier. Ultrasound findings, including fluid, the babies’ bladders and blood-flow or heart findings, guide the assessment. Growth restriction and TTTS can coexist, but they are not interchangeable labels.

TTTS needs specialist assessment because it can become serious. The appropriate treatment depends on gestation and the detailed findings. Do not try to correct a suspected blood-flow imbalance with a particular food, extra drinking or bed rest; keep the specialist appointments and ask how to reach the team between visits.

What a low birthweight can mean after birth

A small or premature baby may need extra help with temperature control, feeding, blood glucose or breathing, and may be more vulnerable to infection or difficulty gaining weight. Prematurity also affects maturity, so two babies with the same weight can need different care if born at different gestations. The neonatal team assesses the whole baby, not just the number on the scales.

Some twins stay with their parent on a postnatal ward. Others receive transitional care or spend time in a neonatal unit. It is not correct that almost every low-birthweight baby automatically needs intensive care. The level of support depends on clinical needs and the facilities available.

One twin may need more support or stay in hospital longer than the other. If tube feeding, an incubator or breathing equipment is needed, ask what each part is doing and how you can participate. Staff can help with expressing milk, feeding choices and safe contact according to each baby’s condition.

Useful steps during the pregnancy

Attend the appointments arranged for your pregnancy type and ask for a clear scan schedule. Seek individual nutrition advice if you are struggling to eat, have ongoing vomiting, have a deficiency or need help with diabetes care. There is no single food that guarantees a particular fetal weight or fixes a placental problem.

Routine bed rest is not recommended simply to prevent preterm birth in a multiple pregnancy. Follow your own team’s advice if a particular complication affects activity, and ask them to explain the reason and duration of any restriction. Do not place yourself on bed rest because an online weight chart is worrying.

Contact maternity care promptly for possible labour before term, leaking fluid, bleeding, reduced or changed movements, severe headache, visual disturbance or significant upper abdominal pain. Know the number to use overnight. Regular care improves the chance of finding a problem early, but it cannot guarantee that all complications or low birthweights will be prevented.

Questions that make growth results easier to understand

At the next appointment, ask which placenta/sac type you have, whether each baby is following an expected growth pattern, and whether a difference between them changes the plan. Ask what the fluid and blood-flow findings show, not only the estimated weights.

If an earlier birth is being discussed, ask about the reason, preparation for prematurity and where both babies can receive appropriate care. A written plan can help you explain the situation to a support person without having to remember every number. Growth complications are not a judgement on your effort or a sign that you have failed to feed your babies.

Evidence-informed guidance

What trusted health organizations recommend

WHO defines low birthweight as less than 2,500 g. Weight, gestational age and growth restriction are related but distinct; none should be substituted for an individual neonatal assessment.

Twin guidance bases surveillance and planned birth on placental/sac type and complications. TTTS needs ultrasound-based specialist assessment, not diagnosis from a weight difference alone.

How BeMama can help

Keep questions and the agreed monitoring plan together so both babies’ findings are easy to discuss. BeMama cannot calculate a safe delivery date from an estimated weight or replace fetal-medicine assessment.

When to seek help

Contact maternity care promptly for bleeding, leaking fluid, possible early labour, changed movements or symptoms concerning for pre-eclampsia. Follow the personalised plan for growth concerns or shared-placenta complications.

Evidence notes updated: October 7, 2026

Key takeaways

  • Twins can weigh more than 2.4 kg; there is no universal maximum or ideal target.
  • Placenta and sac arrangement determines important parts of monitoring.
  • Prematurity, growth restriction and TTTS are different clinical issues.
  • Low birthweight does not automatically mean intensive care for every baby.
  • Birth timing and care plans should be based on the whole pregnancy, not a number alone.

Frequently asked questions

Should both twins weigh 2.4 kg?

No. That is neither a required target nor an upper limit. Birthweight varies, and your team considers gestation and each baby’s growth and health.

What counts as low birthweight?

A birthweight below 2,500 g. This definition applies regardless of gestational age and does not, by itself, tell you why a baby is small or what care they will need.

Can identical twins have separate placentas?

Yes. Some identical twins are DCDA, with separate placentas and sacs. The early scan’s placenta and membrane assessment is important for care even before you know whether the twins are identical.

Is one twin being smaller always dangerous?

Not necessarily. The team looks at the difference, each baby’s growth over time, fluid and blood-flow findings. Ask what the measurements mean in your pregnancy rather than relying on a comparison alone.

Does a weight difference mean TTTS?

No. TTTS is a shared-placenta circulation problem assessed with ultrasound findings. Unequal growth can have other causes, and the two conditions can sometimes occur together.

Why might birth be planned before 40 weeks?

Continuing the pregnancy can become riskier than birth for some twin pregnancies. Recommended timing depends on placenta/sac type, complications and local guidance; reaching a specific weight is not the only consideration.

Will both babies have to go to intensive care?

Not necessarily. Some remain on the postnatal ward, some receive transitional support and some need neonatal care. The babies can have different needs and different discharge dates.

Can extra food or bed rest guarantee bigger babies?

No. Adequate nutrition matters, but food cannot correct every placental or growth problem. Routine bed rest is not recommended just to prevent preterm birth in twins; discuss your individual needs with the team.

Does a twin pregnancy always mean a caesarean birth?

No. Placental/sac type, fetal positions, gestation, complications and preferences guide the decision. Ask why a particular mode of birth is recommended for you.

This article is general education, not medical advice, diagnosis, or treatment. Always talk with a qualified healthcare professional about your situation, and seek urgent care for emergencies.
